keyVerseText: And say unto Tyrus, O thou that art situate at the entry of the sea, which art a merchant of the people for many isles, Thus saith the Lord GOD; O Tyrus, thou hast said, I am of perfect beauty. of perfect: Heb. perfect of beauty
rootMeaning: The word מְבוֹאָה (mᵉbôwʼâh) is the feminine form of מָבוֹא (mâbôwʼ), which fundamentally conveys the idea of an entry or entrance. Its root sense emphasizes the act or place of coming in, highlighting a point of transition or arrival. Beyond the simple English gloss of "entry," the root carries a spatial and directional nuance, sometimes associated with the west or sunset, underscoring a movement towards a particular boundary or threshold.
usageInScripture: This term appears only once in Scripture, translated as "at the entry," indicating a specific location or position. Its singular occurrence in Ezekiel 27:3 situates it concretely as a place of approach or access, in this case related to the sea. The consistent translation focusing on entry or entrance reveals its primary function as a marker of a point of arrival or access rather than a general location or abstract concept.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מְבוֹאָה as an entrance or point of coming in enriches our grasp of biblical imagery concerning access and approach, both physically and spiritually. In Scripture, entrances often symbolize opportunities for encounter with God, new beginnings, or divine provision. From a Christ-centered perspective, this word reminds believers that Christ is the true entry point to life and fellowship with God, the gateway through which we come into His presence. The notion of an entry also invites reflection on vigilance and readiness to enter God's kingdom, emphasizing the importance of recognizing and responding to divine invitation.
keyVerseReflection: Ezekiel 27:3 describes Tyre as situated "at the entry of the sea," highlighting its strategic and commercial position. The use of מְבוֹאָה here underscores Tyre's role as a gateway or point of access for maritime trade. This word enriches the verse by portraying Tyre not just as a city by the sea but as a vital threshold through which many peoples and goods pass, emphasizing its significance in the broader narrative of God's dealings with nations.
